core_obligations: Argue by descending induction on a = min(n_i), with the base case that F^n = 0 for n at least a, where the zero complex satisfies the conclusion (proof lines 38561-38564).

After renumbering, assume n_1 = ... = n_r = a and n_i greater than a for i greater than r, choose a basis b_j of F^a and a finite subset J' of the index set such that all f_i with i at most r lie in the span of the b_j with j in J' (proof lines 38564-38568).
Choose a basis c_k of F^{a+1} and a finite subset K' such that the differential of every b_j with j in J' lands in the span of the c_k with k in K' (proof lines 38569-38571).

Apply the induction hypothesis to the elements c_k with k in K' and the elements f_i with i greater than r, obtaining a subcomplex H of F containing them, and set G equal to H in degrees greater than a and equal to the span of the b_j with j in J' in degree a (proof lines 38572-38576).
Verify that the resulting G is a subcomplex of F containing all the given elements, bounded and consisting of finite free modules, which is the conclusion of the lemma (proof lines 38576-38578).
proof_roadmap: Induct downwards on the minimal degree a of the given elements, using the zero complex when F vanishes above a (proof lines 38562-38564).
Take a finite set of basis elements of F^a capturing the elements in degree a and a finite set of basis elements of F^{a+1} capturing their differentials (proof lines 38566-38571).
Apply the induction hypothesis in degree a+1 and glue the two pieces together into the subcomplex G, then read off all the asserted properties (proof lines 38572-38578).
difficulty_reason: The statement takes a bounded above complex F of free R-modules and a finite list of elements f_i in various degrees, and asserts the existence of a bounded subcomplex G of F containing all of them whose terms are finite free (statement lines 38552-38559). The proof is a descending induction on the minimal degree that occurs, and the induction step has to handle two degrees at once: a finite set of basis elements of F^a is chosen to capture the given elements of that degree, and a second finite set of basis elements of F^{a+1} is chosen so that the differentials of the first set land inside the span of the second, which is exactly what makes the glued object a subcomplex rather than just a family of submodules (proof lines 38564-38576). The finite rank and the boundedness of the result come from the finiteness of the two chosen sets and from the induction hypothesis.
